Squatting as a crime

Yes, it is a crime. The Georgia Squatter Reform Act, House Bill 1017 of the 2024 session, created O.C.G.A. 16-7-21.1. A person commits unlawful squatting by entering the land or premises of another and residing there for any period of time, knowing the owner, rightful occupant or an authorized representative has not consented.

Residing simply means inhabiting or living on or within the land or premises. The offense is a misdemeanor punished under 17-10-3. The Act took effect when the governor approved it.

The same bill also changed the magistrate court's reach. That court may now try unlawful squatting violations and hear the owner's intruder proceedings under Code Sections 44-11-30 through 44-11-33.

What an accused squatter can do

Show paperwork. Anyone accused receives a citation telling them to present, within three business days, properly executed documentation authorizing their entry. The head of the issuing law enforcement agency, or a designee, receives it.

Acceptable documents include a properly executed lease or rental agreement, or proof of rental payments. A person who cannot produce anything is subject to arrest.

A person who does submit documents gets a hearing within seven days. If the court finds the documents were not properly executed or have no merit, that person can be subject to removal, arrest and penalties under 16-9-1 and 16-9-2, and an additional fine based on the fair market monthly rent of the property.

Police or a court?

Both play a part. Law enforcement issues the citation that starts the three business day clock, and the head of that agency or a designee receives the occupant's documents. The courts take over if the paperwork is challenged: the magistrate court can try unlawful squatting violations and run the owner's intruder proceedings.

Proceedings on a writ of possession are not required to be jury trials. For an owner, the practical effect is a faster, more local forum than a full civil suit, since the magistrate court sits in the county where the property is.

How an owner removes an occupant

The owner, an agent, or an attorney in fact signs an affidavit before an officer authorized to administer oaths. The affidavit says the owner claims possession in good faith and that a named person has no good faith claim and still refuses to leave. It goes to the sheriff or a deputy, constable, marshal, or another person certified by the Georgia Peace Officer Standards and Training Council in the county where the land lies.

  • The officer exhibits the affidavit to the occupant at the earliest possible day.
  • Three days after the affidavit was exhibited, the officer turns the occupant out of possession.
  • The occupant may instead hand over a counteraffidavit claiming a good faith legal right to possession, and the officer may administer that oath.
  • With a counteraffidavit, neither party is moved. Both affidavits go to the court clerk for a nonjury trial in magistrate court.
  • If the court finds the counteraffidavit not meritorious by a preponderance of the evidence, the occupant is turned out under a writ of possession as soon as practicable.
  • The court may award the plaintiff fair market rent for the length of the occupancy and other relief it finds appropriate.

Forms and filing details are handled by the magistrate court clerk in your county, so ask that office what it needs. A Georgia attorney can help when facts are disputed, such as a claimed oral lease.

How long someone must occupy land before claiming it

Twenty years in ordinary cases, or seven years when the possessor holds color of title. O.C.G.A. 44-5-163 sets twenty years and 44-5-164 sets seven. Color of title means a flawed written document, such as a deed from someone who lacked authority to convey.

Time alone does not do it. The possessor needs actual possession, open and notorious possession, exclusive possession, an uninterrupted period for the entire time the law requires, and a claim of right. Trimming the hedges on a neglected lot next door earns no one ownership.

Possession must also be without the true owner's permission, and government land is traditionally immune from adverse possession. Someone who occupies with the owner's consent, such as a tenant, is not in adverse possession, since consent defeats the claim.

The main rules side by side

The criminal rule, the removal procedure and the ownership doctrine answer different questions, and they can overlap in a single dispute.

Squatting, removal and adverse possession rules
QuestionGeorgia rule
Is residing without consent an offense?Yes, a misdemeanor under 16-7-21.1
How fast must an accused person show documents?Within three business days of the citation
When can an officer remove an intruder?Three days after the affidavit is exhibited, absent a counteraffidavit
Years to claim title without a deedTwenty years (44-5-163)
Years to claim title with color of titleSeven years (44-5-164)
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Georgia houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Proving ownership after years of possession

Not simply by saying so. Apart from color of title, an adverse possessor holds no written proof of ownership, and one who tries to sell will probably have difficulty establishing title. The usual route is a quiet title action in which the possessor asks a court to declare ownership, backed by affidavits or witnesses on the length and nature of possession. A judgment can then support later sales.

For an owner, that means a long-running occupation of part of your land, a fence line or an abandoned strip, is worth addressing early. Written permission, a recorded survey, and a conversation with a Georgia attorney protect your title before the period matures.

Selling with an unwanted occupant

Start with the paper trail. Gather the deed, any lease or rent receipts, and written notices you sent, because the squatting statute turns on what documents the occupant can produce.

Then decide the route. If the person entered without any permission, the affidavit and removal procedure above, or a report to law enforcement under the unlawful squatting offense, may fit. If the person once had a lease or paid rent, the facts look more like a tenancy, and the Georgia landlord and eviction rules apply instead. Our landlord tenant guide and eviction notice guide cover that path.

Buyers and title companies want a clear occupancy before closing, so removal of the occupant is normally a condition of any sale of the house.

Frequently asked questions

Can a squatter take ownership of my Georgia house?

Only by meeting every element of adverse possession for the full period: twenty years, or seven years with color of title. The possession must be open, exclusive, uninterrupted, hostile to the owner and under a claim of right.

How quickly can a squatter be removed in Georgia?

Three days after the sheriff or other certified officer shows the owner's affidavit to the occupant, unless the occupant files a counteraffidavit. A counteraffidavit sends the dispute to a nonjury magistrate court trial.

What documents can an accused squatter use?

A properly executed lease or rental agreement or proof of rental payments, presented within three business days of the citation. If the documents are submitted, a hearing is set within seven days.

Does the owner recover rent from a squatter?

Possibly. If the court finds the counteraffidavit not meritorious, it may award fair market rent for the duration of the occupancy and other monetary relief. A person whose documents fail at the seven day hearing can face an added fine based on monthly fair market rent.

Does a quitclaim deed give someone ownership after seven years?

That is no longer so simple, and more documentation than the deed is required. Seven years applies only when the possessor holds color of title and meets every possession requirement.

Georgia Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights: Rules for Selling a Rental

Who settles landlord and tenant disputes

No state agency does. Georgia has no government office with power to step into a rental dispute or compel either side to act. People who cannot settle a disagreement go to court, on their own or with a lawyer.

The Department of Community Affairs hosts a Landlord-Tenant Handbook, which Georgia State University and the University of Georgia have edited and updated since 2021. English and Spanish PDFs are posted. A seller with a tenant in the house, or an owner thinking about renting one out, can use it as a plain-language baseline for the points below.

Security deposit limits

A landlord may not demand more than two months of rent as a deposit. Owners of more than ten rental units, counting units held by a spouse or children, and owners who hire a management agent face extra duties.

  • Deposits go into a bank escrow account used only for that purpose, or the owner posts a bond with the superior court clerk. Tenants get written notice of where the money sits.
  • Before accepting a deposit, the owner hands over a written list of existing damage, lets the tenant check it, and both sides sign.
  • After a lease ends, the landlord has three business days, or a reasonable time after learning the tenant left, to inspect and list damage with estimated costs.

The tenant may inspect during the first five business days after termination and should sign the list or write down what is disputed. A tenant who gave proper notice and owes nothing is entitled to the deposit back within thirty days. Ordinary wear and tear cannot be charged against it.

When the owner sells a rental

The deposit travels with the sale. The former owner either passes it to the new owner, who then answers for it, or returns it to the tenant. A tenant left without either can sue, and it helps to write to both owners first to ask about the money.

The lease itself generally stays in place too. An apartment complex that changes hands is usually bound by existing leases, so new owners cannot raise rent or alter rules mid-term. A seller handing over an occupied rental should give the buyer the signed lease, the deposit amount and the move-in damage list. Gathering those three items before listing saves a scramble at closing.

Notice to end a month-to-month tenancy

A landlord needs to give sixty days, and a tenant needs to give thirty. This arrangement is called a tenancy-at-will, and it also requires sixty days' notice before a changed rent amount takes hold.

Common notice and response periods
SituationPeriodWho acts
Landlord ends a tenancy-at-will60 daysLandlord
Tenant ends a tenancy-at-will30 daysTenant
New rent for a tenant-at-will60 daysLandlord
Leaving early with a court protection order30 daysTenant
Reply to an eviction summons7 days from serviceTenant
Tender of rent and court costs, usable once per 12 months7 days after serviceTenant

Fixed-term leases run by their own wording, and a landlord filing for eviction must follow that wording on notice and termination.

Leaving a lease early

A tenant can leave early only on the lease's terms, with narrow exceptions for service members relocating on orders and tenants fleeing family violence. A tenant who abandons the unit without a lawful reason may owe the landlord money.

Early termination fees are allowed when three conditions hold: the landlord's loss is hard to estimate, both sides meant the fee to cover damages and not to punish, and the amount is a reasonable estimate. If the tenant leaves without permission, the landlord is not required to find a new tenant. The unit can sit empty while the tenant stays on the hook for rent through the end of the lease, unless the landlord accepts the departure.

If the property is foreclosed

Foreclosure ends the original landlord-tenant relationship, and the lender or new owner can pursue an eviction. A tenant is not removed automatically, and a new owner may choose to set up a fresh arrangement. An owner who wants the tenant out still has to give notice.

One trap: if a new owner has started eviction proceedings and then takes or asks for rent, a valid tenancy-at-will can result. Everyone involved should keep written notices.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Georgia houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Repairs a landlord owes

A rental must be kept safe, habitable and in good repair. That means maintaining the building structure, keeping electric, heating, cooling and plumbing working, and using ordinary care to keep the unit safe.

A lease cannot excuse those duties or declare that the landlord need not follow local laws or Georgia's deposit rules. Tenants should report problems promptly, in writing if possible and in the manner the lease requires. Problems that were obvious at move-in are usually the tenant's, unless they make the unit unsafe or uninhabitable.

Retaliation for repair requests or code complaints is unlawful. Filing for eviction, reducing services or raising rent soon afterward is presumed retaliatory unless the landlord shows a lawful reason, such as unpaid rent or serious lease violations.

How an eviction case unfolds

It begins with a demand for possession. The demand does not have to be written unless the reason is unpaid rent, and no special words are needed. The landlord then files a dispossessory affidavit, most often in magistrate court, though state, superior and some municipal courts can hear one.

After service, the tenant has seven days to answer, and the answer should include every defense and counterclaim. Without an answer the court can order the tenant out and send the sheriff.

  • In a nonpayment case, paying the full alleged amount plus court costs within seven days stops the eviction, but only once in a twelve-month stretch.
  • If the landlord will not take the money, the tenant says so in the answer.
  • A court finding a proper offer can require the landlord to accept payment made within three days of its ruling.

Courts may require or suggest mediation before the hearing. A mediator does not decide the case.

Fair housing, lead paint and squatters

Fair housing law protects classes including race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status and disability, and a landlord must allow reasonable accommodations for tenants with disabilities.

Owners renting units built before 1978 must disclose known lead-based paint and hazards in the unit and common areas unless a state-certified inspector finds none. A squatter is someone who never had the owner's permission to enter. The owner can swear an affidavit to have that person removed without an eviction case, and the squatter may face criminal penalties. People who stay past a lease are covered by the dispossessory steps above.

Free legal help comes from the Georgia Legal Services Program, Atlanta Legal Aid Society in Fulton, DeKalb, Cobb, Gwinnett and Clayton counties, and georgialegalaid.org.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Can a Georgia landlord charge a deposit of three months' rent?

No. A landlord cannot require a security deposit worth more than two months of rent.

Does a tenant have to leave when the landlord sells the house?

Not automatically. New owners are generally subject to existing leases, and a tenant-at-will is owed sixty days of notice from the landlord.

How long does a landlord have to return a deposit in Georgia?

Thirty days when the tenant gave proper notice and left owing nothing. Normal wear and tear cannot be deducted.

Can a tenant stop an eviction by paying what is owed?

Yes, in nonpayment cases, if the tenant pays the alleged rent, fees and court costs within seven days of service. This works once in any twelve-month period.

Who can I call for free help with a rental dispute?

The Georgia Legal Services Program covers most of the state, and Atlanta Legal Aid Society serves Fulton, DeKalb, Cobb, Gwinnett and Clayton counties. Georgialegalaid.org has self-help guides.

title: Georgia Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House
content:
Georgia Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House

Cash Home Buyers in Georgia
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Georgia Eviction Notice Rules: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Georgia Eviction Notice Rules sale
  • Turn the Georgia Eviction Notice Rules offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Georgia House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Georgia?
We buy Georgia houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Notice a Georgia landlord must give before an eviction

A Georgia landlord must first demand that the tenant give up the home. For unpaid rent the landlord must also hand over a written pay-or-quit notice at least three business days before going to court. For other reasons the demand can be spoken, and no particular wording is required.

A spoken demand is hard to prove later, so landlords should record when and how they delivered it. A good notice is dated, names the tenant and the address, lists the lease term that was broken, and sets a number of days to leave. The lease may add its own notice or termination rules, which makes it the first paper to pull out, whether you are the landlord or the tenant.

  • The tenant's name and the rental address
  • The date of the notice and the way it was delivered
  • The lease term that was violated, or the rent and fees owed
  • The number of days the tenant has to surrender the home

The three business day rent notice

For back rent and fees, the landlord serves a written demand, and three business days must pass before a dispossessory case can be filed over money. The notice can go out by any method named in the lease, or it can be posted on the unit door in a sealed envelope.

The court affidavit that follows must say the landlord demanded possession and was refused, and where rent is the reason it must confirm the three day notice was given. After the case papers are served, the tenant has seven days to pay what the affidavit claims plus court costs. Paying in full ends the case, but this tender defense can be used only once in any twelve month period with the same landlord.

Once a rent case is filed, a landlord normally stops accepting rent so that no payment can be used as a defense. If the case runs longer than two weeks, the landlord can ask the court to order the tenant to pay rent into the court registry while it waits.

Ending a month-to-month tenancy

A landlord ending a tenancy at will must give sixty days of notice, and a tenant ending one must give thirty days. The same sixty days applies when a landlord wants to keep the tenant but change the rent, since that starts a new tenancy at will.

A fixed lease can slide into this arrangement. If the lease runs out, the tenant stays, and the landlord keeps taking monthly rent, a tenancy at will arises on the old lease terms, and the sixty and thirty day rules take over. A private landlord does not have to give a reason for declining to renew unless the lease requires one, as long as no discrimination law is broken.

One narrow exception favors tenants. A tenant who holds a court order protecting them or their minor children in a family violence or stalking situation may end a lease on thirty days of notice.

Which notice or deadline fits each situation

Georgia landlord and tenant timing
SituationNotice or deadlineWho acts
Unpaid rent or feesWritten notice, then three business days before filingLandlord
Other lease violation or holdoverDemand for possession, spoken or writtenLandlord
Ending a tenancy at willSixty daysLandlord
Leaving a tenancy at willThirty daysTenant
Answering the court papersSeven days from actual serviceTenant
Paying rent and costs to stop the caseSeven days after serviceTenant
Moving after a ruling for the landlordWrit requires the tenant to move after seven daysCourt and sheriff

After the notice period ends

The landlord files a sworn dispossessory affidavit, usually in magistrate court in the county where the rental sits, and the papers are served on the tenant. In most counties the sheriff serves them by handing them to the tenant, giving them to an adult living in the home, or tacking a copy on the door and mailing one.

The tenant then has seven days from actual service to answer, and the clerk will take the answer orally or in writing. When the seventh day lands on a weekend or legal holiday the deadline moves to the next business day. With no answer, the court can order the tenant out and send the sheriff, and a default judgment cannot be appealed. When an answer raises a valid defense, a hearing is usually set within about seven days.

A ruling for the landlord leads to a writ of possession, which is a separate document from the order. The sheriff generally supervises the removal, and the landlord pays for it.

Can a Georgia landlord skip the notice and change the locks?

No. A landlord cannot remove a tenant or block access without going through the court process, even when rent is unpaid. A tenant is entitled to stay with active utilities until the court decides.

Georgia also presumes retaliation when a landlord files for eviction, raises rent, cuts services or ends a lease within three months after a tenant asks for repairs, reports a code violation, or takes part in a tenant group. A landlord can rebut that with a lawful reason such as unpaid rent, serious misconduct or a holdover. A tenant who wins a retaliation claim may recover one month of rent plus $500, court costs and possibly attorney fees.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Georgia houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling a house with a tenant or eviction case

An eviction adds steps that a buyer, the owner and the court clerk all need to track, so find out where the case stands before you sign a contract. Ask the magistrate court clerk in the county where the house sits whether a dispossessory case is open, and ask a Georgia attorney whether the lease continues after a sale.

When someone new buys a rental, the former owner must either move the security deposit to the new owner or refund it to the tenant. A tenant who is owed the deposit can sue if neither happens. A person who never had the owner's permission to be on the property is treated differently: that person is a squatter, and an owner can swear an affidavit to have a squatter removed without an eviction case.

What a buyer will ask about the tenant

Rented houses change hands often, and an as-is buyer should be asked in writing whether the house will be taken with the tenant in place. If it will, hand over the lease, the deposit amount and a rent history. If the buyer wants the home empty, your timeline depends on the notice rules above, so start with the correct notice for the situation.

A cash buyer can often close faster than a lender-financed one, which helps when a tenant is leaving on a set date. Whatever the plan, get the closing date, the move-out date and the deposit handling written into the contract so no one is guessing.

Frequently asked questions

Does a Georgia landlord have to give written notice before evicting?

Only in the rent case. A demand to leave can be spoken for most reasons, but a landlord must give written notice to pay at least three business days before filing over unpaid rent or fees. Because a spoken demand is hard to prove, a dated paper copy protects both sides.

How much notice does a month-to-month tenant get in Georgia?

Sixty days. A landlord ending a tenancy at will gives sixty days, and a tenant leaving gives thirty days. The sixty day period also applies to a landlord who wants to change the rent on a month-to-month tenant.

How long does a tenant have to respond once court papers arrive?

Seven days from actual service. A tenant who misses that window can lose by default, and a default judgment cannot be appealed. If the seventh day is a weekend or holiday, the answer is due the next business day.

Can a tenant stop an eviction for unpaid rent by paying?

Yes, once. Paying everything the affidavit claims plus court costs within seven days of service is a complete defense, but a tenant can use it only one time in twelve months with the same landlord. The tenant should also file an answer saying the money was paid or offered.

Does selling the house cancel an eviction notice in Georgia?

A sale does not cancel a notice or a lease on its own. The old owner must transfer the security deposit or refund it. Ask the county magistrate court clerk about any open case and consult a Georgia attorney about the lease before closing.
